# title: HIS-201 Exam I — Study Guide Terms

column2: The agricultural revolution began when Mesoamerican farmers domesticated squash about 10,000 years ago and later added beans, tomatoes and especially corn, because drying and storing crops let people settle permanently and, by about 1500 BCE, build larger villages with specialized craftworkers, priests and planned urban centers. (Ch. 1)

Squash was the first crop that Mesoamerican pioneers domesticated about 10,000 years ago, and with corn and beans it became the staple of the Olmecs, Mayas, Aztecs, Hohokam and Ancestral Pueblo peoples and one of the American crops that now make up about three-fifths of the world's crops. (Ch. 1)

The Olmecs of the tropical lowlands of south-central Mexico were the Americas' first city-builders, beginning around 1500 BCE with large plazas, pyramids, enormous basalt heads and the first Mesoamerican ball games, and their influence spread through Mesoamerica before their centers suddenly declined. (Ch. 1)

The Mayas built about 50 cities across the Yucatán Peninsula, Belize, Guatemala and Honduras at their height from the 3rd to 9th centuries CE, where priests created writing, mathematicians identified zero and astronomers made a calendar more accurate than any then existing, before the civilization collapsed by 900 CE. (Ch. 1)

The Aztecs moved into central Mexico in the mid-13th century and by the late 15th century ruled a large tribute empire from Tenochtitlán, an island city of about 250,000, until Hernán Cortés, Native allies and smallpox conquered them in 1519–1521. (Ch. 1–2)

The Mogollon people flourished in southern New Mexico during the 1st millennium CE, farming near streams with floodplain irrigation, and became renowned for exquisite pottery before declining from about the 12th century, when some may have helped build Paquime. (Ch. 1)

The Hohokam people of southern Arizona built the most extensive irrigation canals in precontact North America along the Salt and Gila Rivers, along with ball courts, to support large desert populations growing beans, squash and maize until their centers declined by about the 14th century. (Ch. 1)

Anasazi is the former label for the Ancestral Pueblo peoples of the Four Corners (Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico and Utah), who adapted corn, beans and squash to the high Colorado Plateau, built multistory masonry towns such as Chaco Canyon and Mesa Verde, and peaked around 900–1100 CE with about 30,000 people. (Ch. 1)

Chaco Canyon in New Mexico was the largest Ancestral Pueblo settlement center, linked by hundreds of miles of straight, wide roads and built with more than 200,000 hauled trees, and its Fajada Butte spiral glyph, studied by Anna Sofaer in 1977, marked solstices, equinoxes and lunar cycles as an ancient calendar. (Ch. 1)

The Eastern Woodlands were the river valleys, Great Lakes and Atlantic coast of eastern North America, where most peoples lived mainly on abundant animals, fish and nuts, built mounds such as those of the Adena, Hopewell and Mississippians, and added farming (gourds, pumpkins and later maize) that eventually supported cities like Cahokia. (Ch. 1)

The Hopewell people, with the Adena, built burial mounds in the Ohio and Mississippi valleys about 2,000 years ago for leading men and women, and graves holding copper, mica, shells and pearls from Canada, Wyoming and Florida show the Eastern Woodlands' extensive trade and religious complexity. (Ch. 1)

The Subarctic was the forested region of Canada with only about 100 frost-free days a year, where eastern Algonquian and western Athapaskan peoples lived by hunting and fishing, moving from summer fishing camps to fall berry patches to winter moose and caribou grounds. (Ch. 1)

In the Amazon rainforest Native farmers cultivated food-producing trees for thousands of years, domesticating more than 70 tree species, creating at least one-eighth of the nonflooded forest and enriching up to one-tenth of its soils with charcoal, showing how Native peoples reshaped their environments. (Ch. 1)

Because Eurasians had lived for centuries beside domesticated animals that bred diseases like smallpox and measles while Native Americans had few such animals and no acquired immunity, European diseases after 1492 became the main killer of millions of Indians, as smallpox's "virgin soil epidemics" did in central Mexico in 1520–1521 and among the Hurons in the 1630s. (Ch. 1–2, 4)

Paquime, in present-day Chihuahua, Mexico, was a trading city built around 1300 (possibly with Mogollon help) with more than 2,000 rooms, advanced water and sewage works, mounds and ball courts, and it linked a huge Southwestern trade network in macaws, turkeys, feathers, turquoise, shells and copper until its 15th-century decline. (Ch. 1)

The Pueblos were the Arizona and New Mexico villages, and the peoples in them, founded by Four Corners refugees after the Ancestral Pueblo decline and named by the Spaniards, who later conquered them under Oñate in 1598 until Popé's Pueblo Revolt of 1680 drove Spain out of New Mexico. (Ch. 1–3)

The Navajos were Athapaskan speakers from western Canada and Alaska who reached the Southwest one or two centuries before European contact, and together with the Apaches they raided and were enslaved by Spanish New Mexico, becoming important peoples of the postcontact Southwest. (Ch. 1, 3)

The Natchez of the lower Mississippi Valley kept Mississippian temple mounds and a ranked society led by a chief called the "Great Sun," and in 1729 they rose up with some newly arrived African slaves against French Louisiana, killing or capturing about 500 colonists. (Ch. 1, 5)

The Iroquois were Iroquoian-speaking farmers and hunters of the Northeast who lived in semipermanent towns of longhouses and traced descent through women, and their five-nation League, armed with Dutch guns, waged the Beaver Wars that destroyed the Hurons in 1648–1649. (Ch. 1, 4)

The Hurons were an Iroquoian-speaking confederacy of 20,000 farmers near Georgian Bay who became New France's chief fur-trade allies under Samuel de Champlain, until smallpox halved their population in 1634–1640 and well-armed Iroquois destroyed their towns in 1648–1649. (Ch. 1, 4)

The Cherokees were southern Iroquoian speakers of the Southeast who became one of the Indian confederacies, with the Creeks, Choctaws and Chickasaws, that Carolina traders encouraged to raid each other for captives in the Indian slave trade. (Ch. 1, 3)

The Algonquins lived along the Atlantic coast and Great Lakes in smaller, patrilineal communities than the Iroquois, farming from southern New England to Virginia, and their peoples included the roughly 100,000 coastal Indians of New England and the trading allies of New France. (Ch. 1, 4–5)

The Tainos were the Caribbean people of the Greater Antilles, ruled by caciques, whom Christopher Columbus met and called "Indians" in 1492 and whose numbers collapsed within one generation from Spanish war, forced labor in mines and fields, malnutrition and Eurasian diseases. (Ch. 1–2)

John Cabot (Giovanni Caboto) was an Italian mariner whom England's Henry VII backed in 1497 to sail from Bristol to a "new-found" island rich in cod, before his second voyage, seeking a Northwest Passage, vanished in 1498. (Ch. 2)

The Northwest Passage was the hoped-for northern sea route through North America to Asia that John Cabot sought on his lost 1498 voyage and that Richard Hakluyt later cited when promoting English colonies to Walter Raleigh. (Ch. 2)

Sugar was the labor-intensive crop that drove the Atlantic slave trade, spreading from Crusader plantations to Portugal's Atlantic islands worked by West African slaves, then to Spanish and English Caribbean plantations whose sugar earned England more than all its mainland colonies combined. (Ch. 2–3)

Slavery became the labor system of European colonies as sugar planters turned to enslaved Africans, Spain forced Indians and Africans into mines and plantations, and Chesapeake and Carolina planters switched from indentured servants to African slaves after 1680, until by 1775 one in five Americans was of African ancestry. (Ch. 2–3, 5)

A plantation was a large estate growing one cash crop with intensive forced labor, beginning with Crusader and Portuguese sugar plantations worked by slaves and spreading to Caribbean sugar, Chesapeake tobacco and South Carolina rice, which made African slavery the dominant labor system of the colonial South. (Ch. 2–3, 5)

Christopher Columbus was an Italian navigator whom Spain's Ferdinand and Isabella backed after Portugal rejected him, and his October 12, 1492, landing at San Salvador and voyages to Cuba and Hispaniola began permanent contact between the hemispheres and Spain's conquest of the Tainos. (Ch. 2)

Spain, united under Ferdinand and Isabella, led European colonization of the Americas after backing Columbus in 1492, conquering the Aztecs and Incas, enriching itself with silver and sugar through a centralized royal bureaucracy, and later holding northern borderlands in New Mexico, Florida, Texas and California with missions and presidios. (Ch. 2–3, 5)
Amerigo Vespucci was the writer who called the lands Columbus had reached Mundus Novus, the "New World," and a German mapmaker named the continents "America" in his honor. (Ch. 2)

Hernán Cortés was the Spanish conquistador who in 1519 exploited Aztec enemies to raise a huge Native army, seized Emperor Moctezuma, and with the help of smallpox besieged Tenochtitlán until it surrendered in August 1521. (Ch. 2)

The Incas built a powerful empire in the Andes of South America whose engineers terraced hills and mountains for farming, but Francisco Pizarro and his brothers conquered it by 1532 through Inca political divisions, disease, technology and luck, giving Spain the silver-rich Andes. (Ch. 1–2)

The Columbian exchange was the continuing transfer of American, Eurasian and African plants, animals and germs that began with Columbus's 1492 landfall, sending American crops like corn and potatoes to Europe while bringing horses, pigs, rats and deadly diseases to the Americas. (Ch. 2)

Silver became Spain's greatest American treasure after major strikes in Mexico and South America from the 1540s, as Indians and Black slaves were forced into mines like Potosí (120,000 people by 1570) and about 16,000 tons of silver shipped to Europe in the 16th century, with the Crown taking one-fifth. (Ch. 2)

Álvar Núñez Cabeza de Vaca was a member of Pánfilo de Narváez's failed 1528 Florida expedition who, after years as a captive, escaped with three others, including the Black slave Esteban, across Texas and northern Mexico and reached Mexico City in 1536. (Ch. 2)

Hernando de Soto was a Spaniard enriched by conquering Peru who led a destructive expedition across the Southeast from Florida to Texas looking for imagined riches, and though he found no treasure, he was the last European to see several Mississippian chiefdoms and hastened their shift to decentralized confederacies. (Ch. 2)

Francisco Vázquez de Coronado led 300 Spaniards and 1,000 Mexican Indian warriors into the Southwest in 1539 seeking rich cities but found only modest pueblos, destroyed Pueblo villages, followed "the Turk" onto the Great Plains toward Quivira, and was tried for "great cruelties" after returning in 1542. (Ch. 2)

The Protestant Reformation, begun by Martin Luther in 1517 and extended by John Calvin, split western Christianity into Catholic and Protestant churches, turned European rivalry into religious war, and made colonies outposts of Catholic and Protestant rivalry, from Huguenot Florida to Puritan New England. (Ch. 2)

Catholicism was the religion of the Spanish, Portuguese and French monarchs that Martin Luther and John Calvin attacked over indulgences and church corruption, and in America it drove Spanish Franciscan and French Jesuit missions to convert Indians while Maryland became a Catholic refuge. (Ch. 2–4)

Martin Luther was the German monk who taught "justification by faith alone," posted 95 theses against the sale of indulgences on a Wittenberg church door in 1517, and held that only Scripture was infallible, launching the Protestant Reformation. (Ch. 2)

St. Augustine was the Florida town Pedro Menéndez de Avilés founded in 1565 after destroying the French Huguenot Fort Caroline, and it became the oldest European town in the United States and the anchor of Spanish Florida's missions, surviving Carolina's 1702 attack. (Ch. 2–3)

The Puritans were English Calvinists, mostly Presbyterians and Congregationalists, who wanted to purge the Church of England of bishops and Catholic ceremonies, and when Charles I persecuted them about 21,000 migrated to Massachusetts Bay in 1630–1642 to build a godly "city on a hill." (Ch. 2, 4)

Sir Walter Raleigh was an English sea dog who applied conquest ideas learned in Ireland to North America, sending the 1584 expedition and the failed Roanoke colonies, and was later imprisoned and beheaded under James I. (Ch. 2)

Roanoke was Walter Raleigh's colony on the Outer Banks of present-day North Carolina, where the first 1584 expedition alienated the Roanoke Indians and their chief Wingina, and the 1587 colony under John White vanished, leaving only "CROATOAN" carved on a post in 1590. (Ch. 2)

Virginia, named by Elizabeth I for the "Virgin Queen" during Raleigh's Roanoke venture, became England's first lasting colony at Jamestown in 1607, grew rich on John Rolfe's tobacco, became a royal colony in 1624, and shifted from indentured servants to African slaves after 1680. (Ch. 2–3)

Powhatan was the ruler of a Virginia confederacy of about 20,000 people in some 30 villages who tolerated the Jamestown English to gain their guns and trade goods against Indian rivals and allied with them through his daughter Pocahontas's marriage to John Rolfe in 1614. (Ch. 3)

Jamestown was the Virginia Company's first settlement, founded on Chesapeake Bay in 1607 on a swampy, mosquito-filled peninsula, where disease, refusal to grow food and the "starving time" of 1609–1610 left only 60 survivors before tobacco saved the colony. (Ch. 3)

John Rolfe was the Jamestown colonist who grew a profitable Virginia tobacco for overseas sale, starting the tobacco boom that took over Powhatan's lands, and married Powhatan's daughter Pocahontas in 1614. (Ch. 3)

The Franciscans were Catholic friars, followers of St. Francis of Assisi, who ran Spain's frontier missions, persuading Philip III to keep New Mexico, staffing 40 Florida missions with 26,000 baptized Indians by 1675, and later founding missions in Texas and California. (Ch. 3, 5)

The headright system, created by the Virginia Company in 1618, gave existing colonists 100 acres, new settlers 50 acres, and sponsors 50 acres for each immigrant whose passage they paid, which drew servants and investment into Virginia's tobacco economy. (Ch. 3)

Charles II was the English king restored to the throne in 1660 who granted the Carolinas to proprietors in 1663, gave New Netherland to his brother James, Duke of York, in 1664, and gave Pennsylvania to William Penn in 1681. (Ch. 3–4)

The Navigation Acts (1651, 1660, 1663 and 1673) were English laws that made colonies ship "enumerated commodities" such as tobacco and sugar only to England, route most European imports through England, and pay customs duties, angering Chesapeake planters while New Englanders often ignored them. (Ch. 3–4)

Nathaniel Bacon was a wealthy recent immigrant shut out of Governor William Berkeley's Indian-trade monopoly who in 1676 led Virginia frontier farmers in attacking friendly and hostile Indians alike and burned Jamestown before dying of dysentery, ending Bacon's Rebellion. (Ch. 3)

South Carolina was founded in 1669 by English and Barbadian immigrants at Charles Town, prospered first on the Indian slave and deerskin trade and then on African slaves and rice, survived the 1715 Yamasee War, had a Black majority by 1708, and saw the Stono Rebellion of 1739. (Ch. 3, 5)

The Yamasee War began in 1715 when the Yamasees, fearing Carolina would enslave them next, attacked Carolina traders, posts and plantations and killed hundreds of colonists, so the colony barely survived and the regional Indian slave trade declined. (Ch. 3)

New Netherland was the Dutch West India Company's colony founded in 1624 along the Hudson River, with New Amsterdam on Manhattan and Fort Orange (Albany), whose gun trade armed the Iroquois for the Beaver Wars until Charles II's brother James seized it in 1664 as New York. (Ch. 4)

The Separatists were devout Congregationalists who decided the Church of England was too corrupt to reform, fled persecution to Holland in 1608, and as the Pilgrims founded Plymouth colony in 1620. (Ch. 4)

The Mayflower Compact was the framework of government the Pilgrims drew up aboard the Mayflower before landing at Plymouth in 1620, creating a governor and assistants elected each year by the colony's adult men even though they had no royal charter. (Ch. 4)

The Massachusetts Bay Colony was founded by Puritans of the Massachusetts Bay Company, chartered in 1629, who under Governor John Winthrop founded Boston in 1630, turned the company charter into a representative government, and drew about 21,000 immigrants in family groups by 1642. (Ch. 4)

Salem was the Massachusetts town founded by Puritan advance parties in 1629, where Roger Williams later preached and where the 1692 witchcraft trials, begun by accusations from adolescent girls, led to 20 executions. (Ch. 4)

John Winthrop was the lawyer who became the first governor of the Massachusetts Bay Colony and in 1630 led the Puritan fleet that founded Boston, urging settlers to build a godly "city on a hill" that would be an example to the world. (Ch. 4)

Roger Williams was a Salem minister who demanded a full break with the Church of England, separation of church and state, and insisted the king could not grant land not bought from the Indians, so Massachusetts Bay prepared to deport him and in 1636 he founded Providence, later part of Rhode Island. (Ch. 4)

Anne Hutchinson was a Boston midwife who began explaining minister John Cotton's sermons and adding her own controversial ideas, so Massachusetts Bay's ministers accused her of heresy and expelled her in 1638, and she later died in an Indian attack on Long Island. (Ch. 4)

William Penn was a Quaker leader to whom Charles II granted Pennsylvania in 1681 as a refuge for Quakers, where Penn bought land from the Lenni Lenape before selling it, guaranteed freedom of worship and a representative assembly, and drew 21,000 settlers by 1700. (Ch. 4)

California was Spain's last major colonial project in North America, authorized in 1768 out of fear of Russians moving south from Alaska, where Gaspar de Portolá and Fray Junípero Serra founded presidios and missions, and by 1800 18 Franciscan missions held 13,000 Indian converts. (Ch. 5)

The Scots-Irish were descendants of 17th-century Scots who had settled northern Ireland, and about 250,000 of them came to British North America in the 18th century, mostly moving into the backcountry, where many English colonists saw them as clannish and culturally inferior. (Ch. 5)

The backcountry was the frontier west of the settled seaboard where Germans, Scots-Irish and native-born colonists poured from the 1720s, forming isolated, self-sufficient farms that made it a "society of equals" but sparked ethnic and sectional conflict with the English-dominated coast. (Ch. 5)

The Enlightenment was an intellectual movement begun in Europe in the 17th century that stressed the power of human reason to reveal the laws of nature and society, inspiring Benjamin Franklin's experiments and a "rational Christianity," though it changed few ordinary colonists' lives. (Ch. 5)

The Great Awakening was a mid-18th-century religious revival that began in the 1730s among Presbyterians and Congregationalists, preached the need for a "new birth" through conversion, exploded with George Whitefield's 1739–1741 tour, and spread Presbyterian and Baptist churches through the South and backcountry. (Ch. 5)

George Whitefield was the English "boy preacher" whose dramatic two-year tour from Georgia to New Hampshire starting in fall 1739 drew all classes and races and turned local revivals into the Great Awakening. (Ch. 5)

The middle class, or "middling sort," made up nearly three-quarters of the white population in the colonies compared with less than one-third in England, because cheap land, scarce labor and wages 100% higher than England's let colonists save and own farms. (Ch. 5)

The balanced constitution was England's government of Crown (monarchy), Lords (aristocracy) and Commons (people), which colonists praised as the basis of their liberty but which patronage and bribery corrupted, while colonial governments copied it with a governor, council and elected assembly. (Ch. 5)
